text: What nobody tells you about the self-checkout lane—and here I mean the genuinely no-attendant kind, the kind where the machine's voice has that flattened mid-Atlantic chirp engineered, presumably by some committee of acoustic psychologists in a windowless building in suburban Cincinnati, to be maximally inoffensive and therefore maximally creepy—is that it is a referendum on whether you believe yourself to be a good person. You scan the avocado. The machine does not believe you scanned the avocado. There is a silence, a weighing, during which you become aware that you are being trusted and surveilled simultaneously, which turns out to be the exact emotional texture of late capitalism, or at least of a Tuesday, and you find yourself performing honesty with exaggerated, almost theatrical gestures for the benefit of a camera that may or may not exist, may or may not be watching, may or may not be recording your small humiliations for an audience of nobody, and the worst part, the part that keeps you up, is that you would have paid for the avocado regardless, you wanted to pay, you are not even tempted, and yet the architecture of the thing has made you feel, standing there in your coat, faintly and permanently guilty.

Consider the man who decides, at thirty-four, to become the kind of person who runs—not jogs, the distinction matters to him in a way he could not defend out loud—and who buys the shoes, the technical socks with the little L and R woven in, the watch that records his heart's frantic arithmetic and uploads it to a server in a state he has never visited, so that somewhere a graph of his exertion exists more durably than his exertion did. And the thing he discovers, around mile two, lungs doing their wet accordion thing, is that the running was never about the running; it was about being able to think of himself as someone who runs, a self-conception purchasable in increments, and that the actual physical fact of his body laboring up the incline behind the reservoir is almost an inconvenience, a tax levied on the identity, and he wonders—gasping, ridiculous, sincere—whether everything he has ever wanted has been like this, a real thing he endured only to possess its idea, and whether there is anyone at all, in any of the lit windows he passes, who has figured out how to want the thing itself and not merely its reflection in the imagined eye of some witness who, he suspects, is not even paying attention.

The customer-service representative—and we should pause on that phrase, representative, as though she stands in for the company the way an ambassador stands in for a nation, vested with its dignity, when in fact she is twenty-three and contractually forbidden from saying the words I'm sorry because Legal has determined that apology implies liability—the representative has a script, and the script has branches, and the branches have sub-branches, and somewhere at the bottom of this decision tree, this fractal of corporate caution, is a leaf-node that addresses your specific grievance, which is real, which has cost you money and an afternoon, but which she can reach only by traversing every prior node, asking the questions she already knows are irrelevant, reading the legally-mandated disclosures aloud at a clip designed to defeat comprehension, and you understand—you both understand, this is the unbearable part, the mutual transparent knowing—that the two of you are conscripts in a procedure neither of you authored, performing a play about helpfulness whose actual content is delay, and that her warmth, which is not fake exactly, which is the warmth of a person being kind inside a machine built to prevent kindness from costing anything, is the only genuine thing on the entire call, and it is not enough, and she knows it is not enough, and neither of you can say so.

There is a particular quality of light in waiting rooms, fluorescent and total and shadowless, that seems engineered—though it cannot be, surely no one engineered it, surely it is just the cheapest bulbs purchased in bulk—to abolish the passage of time, so that you sit there with the laminated magazine you are not reading, the one with the curling corner, and you become a creature without history or future, a pure waiting-thing, and the genuinely strange part is how quickly you adapt, how the self that has plans and grievances and a sandwich in the car simply powers down, enters a kind of standby, and you catch yourself an hour later having thought about nothing, literally nothing, a blankness so complete it frightens you in retrospect the way it frightens you to realize you drove the last six miles of a familiar route with no memory of doing it. And you wonder if this is what they mean by peace, the thing the apps with the rain sounds are selling, this evacuation of the striving self, and whether the difference between enlightenment and a waiting room is only that one of them charges a subscription, and whether the receptionist, who has now said your name twice, has been watching you sit there with your mouth slightly open, gone, absent, briefly and accidentally free.

The trouble with sincerity—and I mean this practically, as a problem one actually faces at, say, a dinner where someone asks how you are and means it—is that the moment you decide to be sincere, to really answer, you have introduced a layer of decision, of strategy, that sincerity by definition is not supposed to contain, so that the more carefully you attempt to be authentic the more you are in fact performing authenticity, calibrating it, watching your own face for evidence of its success, and this regress has no floor, you can go down and down, each level of self-awareness generating a fresh layer to be aware of, the watcher watched by a watcher watched in turn, until you suspect that the only people who are ever genuinely sincere are the ones too unreflective to know the word, the ones who blurt, and that the reflective—you, presumably, since you are reading this and nodding, which nod I have now made you self-conscious about—are sentenced to an irony they did not choose and cannot escape, doomed to mean things and to know that they are choosing to mean them, which is not the same, which is maybe the loneliest available distinction, and which I am, you will notice, deploying right now, in this very sentence, sincerely, or sincerely enough.
